title: Functional dependencies and normal forms
subtitle: Bad table design makes data contradict itself. Functional dependencies say exactly which designs are bad.

anom.title: Why design matters: update anomalies
anom.body: Suppose one table holds (student, course, instructor, instructor office). The office is repeated on every enrolment. Change an instructor’s office and you must update many rows — forget one and the data disagrees (update anomaly). A new instructor with no students cannot be recorded (insertion anomaly); deleting the last enrolment loses the instructor’s details (deletion anomaly). Normalisation removes them by splitting tables.

fd.title: Functional dependencies and closure
fd.body: X → Y (a functional dependency) means any two rows that agree on X agree on Y — e.g. studentID → name. The closure X⁺ is everything X determines: start with X and keep adding the right side of any dependency whose left side is already present. For R(A,B,C,D,E) with A→B, B→C, CD→E: A⁺ = ABC... it stops at ABC because E needs D as well.
fd.steps: Is AD a key of R(A,B,C,D,E)? Compute (AD)⁺. AD → B (A→B) → C (B→C) → E (CD→E). Every attribute is reached. Neither A nor D alone reaches everything, so AD is a candidate key (minimal).

keys.title: Finding candidate keys
keys.body: Attributes that appear on no right-hand side must be in every key. Compute their closure; if it covers everything, you are done, otherwise add more attributes. For the example the key is AD. Prime attributes are those in some candidate key.

nf.title: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF
nf.body: 1NF: every cell holds one atomic value. 2NF: 1NF and no partial dependency — no non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key. 3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependency — for every X→A, X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF: for every X→A, X is a superkey (stricter). Examples from the checker: R(A,B,C) with A→B, B→C is 2NF (B→C is transitive); R(A,B,C,D) with AB→C, B→D is 1NF (D depends on part of the key AB); R(A,B,C) with AB→C, C→B is 3NF (C→B is allowed in 3NF since B is prime, but C is not a superkey).

decomp.title: Decomposition
decomp.body: To remove a violation, split the table along the offending dependency: for A→B→C, split R(A,B,C) into R1(A,B) and R2(B,C). A good decomposition is lossless (joining the parts gives back exactly the original — the common attributes must be a key of one part) and ideally dependency-preserving. Denormalising (re-joining) is sometimes chosen deliberately for read speed.
decomp.steps: Decompose R(A,B,C) with A→B, B→C to 3NF. R1(A,B) and R2(B,C). Common attribute B is a key of R2, so the join is lossless.

constraints.title: Integrity constraints and assertions
constraints.body: Domain constraints restrict values (age > 0); key and NOT NULL constraints; referential integrity (foreign keys); CHECK conditions and general assertions; triggers for richer rules. The DBMS refuses updates that violate them.
